statement: A driver travels from one town to another at an average of 60 km/h and returns along the same road at an average of 40 km/h. What is the average speed for the whole journey?

choices.misconception: I averaged the two speeds, which would only be right if equal TIME were spent at each, not equal distance.
I weighted the two speeds by their own values instead of by the time each leg took.
I halved the correct answer, dividing by the total distance twice.
I added the two speeds together, which gives a number faster than either leg and so cannot be an average of them.

hints: Average speed is never the average of two speeds.
Pick a convenient distance, say 120 km each way, and work out the two times.
120/60 = 2 hours out and 120/40 = 3 hours back, so 240 km in 5 hours, which is 48 km/h.

solutions.reliable: Average speed means total distance divided by total time, and here the two legs take different times, so the two speeds cannot simply be averaged. Choose a convenient one-way distance - 120 km works because both speeds divide it - giving 120/60 = 2 hours out and 120/40 = 3 hours back. That is 240 km in 5 hours, so the average is 240/5 = 48 km/h. Notice it is below the midpoint of 50, because more of the journey's TIME is spent at the slower speed. Any distance gives the same answer. The transferable idea: average speed is total distance over total time, and equal distances weight the slower leg more heavily.
solutions.elegant: Equal distances at two speeds give their harmonic mean: 2 x 60 x 40 / (60 + 40) = 4800/100 = 48.

whyOnTest: The plain average is the trap, and knowing the answer must fall below it eliminates two choices instantly.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
